 t_n=\max_{G\in\mathcal R_n}\tau(G).
\]

3	Here is an explicit finite-sum formula. It is computationally extravagant, rather than a short piecewise formula, but it involves only \(n\), integer arithmetic, determinants, least common multiples, and an integer logarithm. In particular, there is no graph optimization on its right-hand side.
4	
5	## Formula
6	
7	The following definitions specify integers and matrices directly from \(n\).
8	
9	Put
10	\[
11	M=\binom n2,\qquad N=2^M,\qquad B=N+1,\qquad
12	P=n^{\,n-2},\qquad Q=\mathop{\mathrm{lcm}}(1,2,\ldots,P).
13	\]
14	
15	List the pairs \((i,j)\), \(0\le i<j<n\), in lexicographic order, numbered \(0,\ldots,M-1\). Write \(k(i,j)\) for the number assigned to \((i,j)\).
16	
17	For each integer \(m\) with \(0\le m<N\), define
18	\[
19	a_{ij}(m)=
20	\left\lfloor\frac{m}{2^{k(i,j)}}\right\rfloor
21	-2\left\lfloor\frac{m}{2^{k(i,j)+1}}\right\rfloor
22	\quad(i<j),
23	\]
24	and set \(a_{ji}(m)=a_{ij}(m)\), \(a_{ii}(m)=0\). Set
25	\[
26	d_i(m)=\sum_{j=0}^{n-1}a_{ij}(m),\qquad
27	L_m=\operatorname{diag}(d_0(m),\ldots,d_{n-1}(m))-(a_{ij}(m)).
28	\]
29	
30	A hat on an index means that its row and column are deleted. Define
31	\[
32	D_m=\det L_m[\widehat0],\qquad
33	F_m=\det L_m[\widehat0,\widehat1],
34	\]
35	and
36	\[
37	z_m=\left\lfloor\frac1{D_m+1}\right\rfloor,\qquad
38	c_m=\left\lfloor
39	\frac1{1+\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}(d_i(m)-d_0(m))^2}
40	\right\rfloor.
41	\]
42	Finally, define
43	\[
44	E_m=
45	c_m(1-z_m)\,n\,d_0(m)\,F_m\,
46	\frac{Q}{D_m+z_m}.
47	\]
48	
49	All the \(E_m\) are nonnegative integers, as proved below. An explicit exact answer to the question is
50	\[
51	\boxed{\displaystyle
52	t_n=\frac1Q
53	\left\lfloor
54	\log_{\,2^{\binom n2}+1}
55	\left(\sum_{m=0}^{\,2^{\binom n2}-1}
56	       \bigl(2^{\binom n2}+1\bigr)^{E_m}\right)
57	\right\rfloor . }\tag{1}
58	\]
59	
60	Formula (1) holds, in fact, for every \(n\ge2\), so it includes the entire requested domain. For example, it gives
61	\[
62	t_{10}=\frac{165}{2}.
63	\]
64	
65	## Proof
66	
67	### 1. Determinants and their bounds
68	
69	The matrix \((a_{ij}(m))\) is the adjacency matrix of a simple labeled graph, and every simple labeled graph occurs exactly once as \(m\) ranges from \(0\) to \(N-1\).
70	
71	For any such graph, its Laplacian satisfies
72	\[
73	x^{\mathsf T}L_mx
74	=\sum_{\{i,j\}:\,a_{ij}(m)=1}(x_i-x_j)^2.
75	\tag{2}
76	\]
77	Consequently, its grounded Laplacian \(L_m[\widehat0]\) is positive definite precisely when the graph is connected. Thus
78	\[
79	D_m>0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\text{the graph is connected};
80	\]
81	otherwise \(D_m=0\).
82	
83	We also need the uniform bound
84	\[
85	0\le D_m\le n^{n-2}=P. \tag{3}
86	\]
87	Indeed, the difference between the Laplacian of \(K_n\) and \(L_m\) is another graph Laplacian, hence is positive semidefinite by (2). After grounding,
88	\[
89	0\preceq L_m[\widehat0]\preceq nI_{n-1}-J_{n-1}.
90	\]
91	Determinants are monotone under this ordering for positive definite matrices; the singular case gives determinant zero. The matrix on the right has eigenvalues \(1,n,\ldots,n\), proving (3).
92	
93	It follows that
94	\[
95	z_m=
96	\begin{cases}
97	1,&D_m=0,\\
98	0,&D_m>0,
99	\end{cases}
100	\]
101	and \(D_m+z_m\) is always an integer between \(1\) and \(P\). Therefore it divides \(Q\).
102	
103	Likewise,
104	\[
105	c_m=
106	\begin{cases}
107	1,&d_0(m)=d_1(m)=\cdots=d_{n-1}(m),\\
108	0,&\text{otherwise}.
109	\end{cases}
110	\]
111	Principal minors of a positive semidefinite matrix are nonnegative. Hence \(F_m\ge0\), and the displayed definition of \(E_m\) indeed gives a nonnegative integer.
112	
113	### 2. The determinant formula for the commute time
114	
115	Consider a connected \(d\)-regular graph, with Laplacian \(L\). Write
116	\[
117	h^v_i=\mathbb E_iT_v.
118	\]
119	These expectations are finite: in a finite connected graph there is, uniformly over starting vertices, a positive probability of reaching \(v\) within \(n-1\) steps.
120	
121	The first-step equations give
122	\[
123	(Lh^v)_i=d\qquad(i\ne v).
124	\]
125	Since the coordinates of \(Lh^v\) sum to zero,
126	\[
127	Lh^v=d\mathbf1-nd\,e_v.
128	\]
129	Therefore, for
130	\[
131	w=\frac{h^0-h^1}{nd},
132	\]
133	we have
134	\[
135	Lw=e_1-e_0. \tag{4}
136	\]
137	
138	Subtracting the constant \(w_0\) from every coordinate allows us to suppose \(w_0=0\). Grounding (4) at vertex \(0\) then yields
139	\[
140	L[\widehat0]\,w_{\widehat0}=e_1.
141	\]
142	The inverse-matrix cofactor formula gives
143	\[
144	w_1-w_0
145	=\frac{\det L[\widehat0,\widehat1]}{\det L[\widehat0]}
146	=\frac FD.
147	\]
148	On the other hand,
149	\[
150	w_1-w_0
151	=\frac{\mathbb E_1T_0+\mathbb E_0T_1}{nd}.
152	\]
153	Thus
154	\[
155	\boxed{\displaystyle
156	\mathbb E_0T_1+\mathbb E_1T_0=nd\,\frac FD.}\tag{5}
157	\]
158	
159	In particular, for each mask \(m\),
160	\[
161	\frac{E_m}{Q}=
162	\begin{cases}
163	\mathbb E_0T_1+\mathbb E_1T_0,
164	 &\text{if its graph is connected and regular},\\
165	0,&\text{otherwise}.
166	\end{cases}\tag{6}
167	\]
168	
169	### 3. Why the fixed pair \(0,1\) suffices
170	
171	Every graph in \(\mathcal R_n\), with any selected distinct vertices \(u,v\), can be labeled so that \(u\) becomes \(0\) and \(v\) becomes \(1\). Its labeled adjacency matrix occurs among our masks.
172	
173	Conversely, every connected regular mask represents a member of \(\mathcal R_n\). Hence (6) proves
174	\[
175	\max_{0\le m<N}E_m=Qt_n. \tag{7}
176	\]
177	
178	### 4. Extracting that integer without a maximum
179	
180	Let
181	\[
182	S=\sum_{m=0}^{N-1}B^{E_m},\qquad E_*=\max_m E_m.
183	\]
184	There are exactly \(N=B-1\) summands, so
185	\[
186	B^{E_*}\le S\le N B^{E_*}<B^{E_*+1}.
187	\]
188	Consequently,
189	\[
190	\lfloor\log_B S\rfloor=E_*.
191	\]
192	Together with (7), this proves (1). ∎
